name: Procedural Memory
question: Has the agent done this kind of task before?
summary: Procedural memory stores how to do things: workflows, checklists, scripts and skills distilled from past successful runs. Instead of rediscovering a multi-step routine every time, the agent retrieves a proven procedure and follows or adapts it, which cuts steps, tokens and errors. It applies to support playbooks and back-office routines as much as to code; research such as Voyager’s skill library and Agent Workflow Memory showed large gains from reusing learned routines.
useCases: Routines the agent repeats: a KYC re-verification, a refund investigation, adding an API endpoint
Team conventions the agent keeps getting wrong
Long workflows with a stable sequence of tool calls

items.detail: facts about the codebase or domain
named, tested code the agent can call
repo-level guides such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md

steps: Log successful trajectories along with the task that triggered them
Distill repeated ones into reusable procedures or scripts, with tests
Index procedures by task description so the agent can retrieve them
Revise or retire procedures when the codebase changes
pitfalls: Stale procedures replay outdated steps with confidence
Retrieving the wrong procedure sends the agent the wrong way
Unreviewed memories can store mistakes or unsafe shortcuts
caption: The second run skips exploration because the working procedure was saved.

code.text: if tests_passed:                  # keep only verified runs
runs = [r for r in LOG if r["kind"] == kind]

steps.title: Log verified runs
steps.text: Record each successful trajectory with the kind of task it solved. Only runs whose tests passed are kept, so mistakes are not memorized.

steps.title: Distill a repeated routine
steps.text: After three runs of the same kind, keep the shortest one as a named skill: four steps plus a check (make test) that proves it worked.

steps.title: Index the skill
steps.text: Store the skill under its description, with the commit it was learned on and a failure counter, so it can be found and audited later.

steps.title: Retrieve at the start of a task
steps.text: A new task, adding a /payouts endpoint, matches the skill with similarity 0.86, above the 0.80 threshold, so the agent loads the skill instead of exploring.

steps.title: Follow it and verify
steps.text: The agent finishes in 4 steps instead of 9 and runs the skill’s check. Verification is what makes reuse safe.

steps.title: Revise or retire
steps.text: After a refactor the skill fails its check twice, so it is retired and the next run explores and learns a fresh version.

pros: Cuts steps, tokens and time on work the agent has done before
Encodes team conventions once instead of correcting them every run
Skills are plain files: reviewable, versioned and shareable
Pairs naturally with verification, so reuse can be checked automatically
cons: Stale skills replay outdated steps with confidence
A loose retrieval threshold loads the wrong procedure
Needs curation: someone must review and retire skills
Little benefit for one-off or highly novel tasks
avoidWhen: Tasks rarely repeat, so there is nothing to reuse
The codebase changes faster than skills can be revalidated

playgroundGuide.scenario: A fintech team’s coding agent has saved one skill, add_api_endpoint, distilled from three verified runs. This week ten tasks arrive. Each has a similarity score between its description and the skill’s. Exploring a task from scratch takes 9 steps; following the skill takes 4; following the wrong skill takes 12, because the agent must backtrack. Each step costs about 3,000 tokens.
controls: Turn the skill library on or off, and say whether the codebase was refactored after the skill was saved.
Choose whether the skill ends with a check (make test) that verifies every reuse.
Drag the retrieval threshold: tasks at or above it load the skill.

outputs.name: Steps per task
outputs.meaning: Total steps ÷ 10 tasks, shown against 9 for exploring everything.

outputs.name: Tasks done correctly
outputs.meaning: Tasks whose change passes its tests.

outputs.name: Skill reused correctly
outputs.meaning: Endpoint tasks that loaded the skill.

outputs.name: Wrong skill retrieved
outputs.meaning: Non-endpoint tasks that loaded it anyway.

outputs.name: Matching tasks missed
outputs.meaning: Endpoint tasks below the threshold, explored from scratch.

presets.name: Loose threshold
presets.expect: Threshold 0.60: 6 correct reuses and 2 wrong retrievals. Expect 6.6 steps per task, 198k tokens and 10 of 10 correct.

presets.name: Tuned threshold
presets.expect: Threshold 0.70: 6 reuses and 1 wrong retrieval. Expect 6.3 steps per task and 189k tokens, the lowest possible here.

presets.name: Too strict
presets.expect: Threshold 0.90: only 1 reuse and 5 endpoint tasks missed. Expect 8.5 steps per task, barely better than exploring.

presets.name: Stale, unchecked skill
presets.expect: Refactored codebase, no check, threshold 0.75: 5 reuses at 4 steps look fast (6.5 steps per task), but only 5 of 10 tasks are correct.

missions.text: Bring the average down to 6.3 steps per task with every task correct.
missions.hint: Wrong retrievals cost 12 steps and missed matches cost 9. Look for the threshold that admits 0.71 but not 0.66.

missions.text: Reuse the skill at least 5 times with no wrong retrievals and every task correct.
missions.hint: The first non-endpoint task scores 0.74. Keep the threshold above it but not above 0.78.

missions.text: After a refactor, keep every task correct while still saving steps over exploring.
missions.hint: Tick the refactor box and keep the skill’s check on: the first failure is caught and the skill is revised.

tools.best: Folders with a SKILL.md file that the agent loads when a task matches the skill’s description.
tools.ex: A skill for adding an API endpoint lists the files to touch, the patterns to copy and ends with make test.
pros: Loaded only when relevant, so it costs no context otherwise
cons: Skills still need someone to keep them current

tools.best: A repository-level instruction file that many coding agents read: build commands, conventions and gotchas.
tools.ex: One AGENTS.md at the repo root tells every agent to run make lint before committing.
cons: Always-on text, so it competes for context
No retrieval or versioning of individual procedures

tools.best: Stateful agents whose memory blocks the agent can read and edit across sessions.
tools.ex: An operations agent keeps an editable runbook block and updates it after each incident.
pros: Memory is a first-class part of the agent
cons: An agent framework to adopt, not a drop-in library
Memory quality still depends on what the agent writes

tools.best: A memory layer that extracts, stores and retrieves facts and preferences for any agent.
tools.ex: A support agent recalls that a merchant settles via NEFT, not UPI, without being told again.
pros: Quick to add to an existing agent
cons: Geared more to facts than step-by-step procedures
Retrieved memories need review for staleness

tools.best: Namespaced long-term memory for LangGraph agents, persisted alongside checkpoints.
tools.ex: Store a distilled workflow per task type and search it by description at the start of each run.
cons: You design the distillation logic yourself

tools.best: Learning how workflows are induced from past trajectories and reused on new web tasks.
tools.ex: Reproduce the paper’s workflow induction on a few of your own logged trajectories.

After the first successful run, the steps are saved as a skill with a checklist, so later runs follow it instead of rediscovering the project layout.

practice.analogy: A recipe card. The first time you cook a dish you experiment; after that you follow the card.

library.name: Claude Code skills
library.what: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file: a name, a description the agent matches tasks against, and the steps.

samples.code:
---
name: add-api-endpoint
description: Add a REST endpoint to the orders service using team conventions.
---

1. Add the route in `services/orders/routes.py`; copy the `/orders/{id}` pattern.
2. Define request and response models in `schemas.py` with Pydantic.
3. Call the service layer only. No database access inside routes.
4. Add tests in `tests/test_routes.py`: one happy path, one 422 validation case.
5. Run `make test` and `make openapi`. Both must pass before you finish.

numericDrill.question: Without a skill a task takes 9 steps; with it, 4. The task runs 20 times a month at about 3k tokens per step. How many tokens does the skill save per month, in thousands?
numericDrill.answer: (9 − 4) steps × 3k tokens × 20 runs = 300k tokens a month, plus fewer chances to go wrong.

interview.question: What's the difference between procedural, semantic and episodic memory for agents?
interview.answer: Procedural memory stores how to do things (workflows, skills). Semantic memory stores facts (codebase conventions, domain knowledge). Episodic memory stores specific past runs. Procedural mostly cuts steps; semantic cuts lookups.

interview.question: How do you keep procedural memories from going stale?
interview.answer: Tie each procedure to tests or checks, record its source and date, re-validate it when related code changes, and retire procedures that start failing.

mistakes.fix: Save only repeated, successful, reviewed procedures
End every skill with a check such as tests passing

quiz.question: Every Monday a coding agent spends 20 minutes rediscovering how the team deploys a hotfix: which branch, which checks, which approvals. What is the most direct fix?
options: Switch to a model with a larger context window
Save the verified deployment routine as a skill the agent retrieves when the task matches
Add more tools to the agent
Lower the model temperature
quiz.explanation: The routine is stable and repeated, which is exactly what procedural memory is for: solve once, reuse many times.

quiz.question: You are writing a skill for “add an API endpoint to the payments service”. What belongs in it? Select all that apply.
options: The files to touch and the patterns to copy
A final check, such as make test, that proves it worked
A specific description of when the skill applies
The full transcripts of every past run
quiz.explanation: A skill is a concise, reusable procedure with a check and a description for retrieval. Raw transcripts are episodic records and waste context.

quiz.question: Without a skill a catalogue-import task takes 11 steps; with it, 5. It runs 30 times a month at about 2,500 tokens per step. How many tokens does the skill save per month?
quiz.explanation: (11 − 5) steps × 2,500 tokens × 30 runs = 450,000 tokens a month.

quiz.question: After a database schema migration, the claims team’s coding agent keeps producing migrations that fail review, always using the same saved procedure. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model has become less capable
The saved procedure is stale and still encodes the old schema
The retrieval threshold is too high
Prefix caching is serving old outputs
quiz.explanation: Stale procedures replay outdated steps with confidence. Track failures per skill and revise or retire it.

quiz.question: At a retrieval threshold of 0.60, the agent loads the “add endpoint” skill for a task about rotating API keys, then wastes steps backtracking. What should you change first?
options: Remove the skill library
Raise the threshold and sharpen the skill’s description, then measure on real tasks
Lower the threshold further
Add the rotation steps to the endpoint skill
quiz.explanation: A loose threshold causes wrong retrievals. Tune it on labelled tasks and make descriptions specific about when the skill applies.

quiz.question: Which details should be stored with each saved skill so it can be audited later? Select all that apply.
options: The commit or date it was learned on
How many times its check has failed
Who reviewed or owns it
Patient records that appeared in the run it came from
quiz.explanation: Provenance and failure counts show when a skill may be stale. Never store sensitive data such as patient records in memory.

quiz.question: A support agent “knows” that the billing service is written in Go and owned by the payments team. Which kind of memory is this?
options: Procedural
Semantic
Episodic
Working
quiz.explanation: Facts about the world or codebase are semantic memory. Procedural memory is how to do something.

quiz.question: An agent recalls that on 3 March it failed to reconcile an exchange trade file because of a time-zone bug. Which kind of memory is this?
options: Episodic
Procedural
Semantic
Parametric
quiz.explanation: A record of a specific past event is episodic memory. Distilled into a rule or routine, it could become procedural.

quiz.question: In the Voyager research agent, what does the skill library contain?
options: Executable programs, retrieved by matching their descriptions to the current task
Fine-tuned copies of the model
Screenshots of past games
A SQL table of rewards
quiz.explanation: Voyager stores working code as skills, indexed by description, and composes them for new tasks.

quiz.question: A Claude Code skill lives in a folder with a SKILL.md file. What mainly decides whether the agent loads it for a task?
options: The size of the folder
The skill’s description matching the task, or the user invoking it by name
The alphabetical order of skills
The time of day
quiz.explanation: The description is what the agent matches against; a skill’s body loads only when it is used.

quiz.question: Exploring takes 9 steps, following the right skill 4, following a wrong skill 12. Of 10 tasks, 6 reuse correctly, 2 load the wrong skill and 2 are explored. What is the average steps per task?
Which are signs that a saved procedure should be revised or retired? Select all that apply.
options: Its check has failed on the last few reuses
An API it calls has been deprecated
It has been reused 200 times successfully
The part of the codebase it touches was refactored
quiz.explanation: Failures, deprecations and refactors signal staleness. Many successful reuses are a reason to keep it.

quiz.question: A team proposes saving every agent trajectory as memory “so nothing is lost”. What is the better policy?
options: Save everything; retrieval will sort it out
Save only repeated routines from verified, successful runs, after review
Save only failed runs, to learn from them
Save nothing and rely on the model
quiz.explanation: Saving everything memorizes mistakes and floods retrieval. Keep verified, reviewed procedures.

quiz.question: When is a repository instruction file such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md enough, without separate skills?
options: For short conventions that apply to almost every task, such as “run make lint before committing”
For long, rarely needed procedures
For storing customer data
Never; skills are always better
quiz.explanation: Always-on files suit short, universal rules. Long procedures belong in skills that load only when relevant.

quiz.question: A skill cuts a task from 8 steps to 3, and it applies to 40% of tasks; the rest still take 8. What is the new average steps per task?
What can go wrong with procedural memory that nobody reviews? Select all that apply.
options: It can store unsafe shortcuts, such as skipping tests
It can replay a mistake on every future run
It can capture secrets that appeared during a run
It makes the model’s weights larger
quiz.explanation: Memory is data the agent trusts. Review it like code. It does not change model weights.

quiz.question: What does the Agent Workflow Memory approach do?
options: Induces reusable workflows from past trajectories and gives them to the agent on new tasks
Compresses the KV cache
Fine-tunes the model on every run
Runs tools in parallel
quiz.explanation: It extracts common sub-routines from past runs and supplies them as guidance, improving success on web-navigation tasks.

quiz.question: Skill descriptions such as “helper for backend stuff” cause poor retrieval. What fixes it?
options: Longer skill bodies
Specific descriptions of what the skill does and when to use it
Randomizing skill order
Removing descriptions entirely
quiz.explanation: Retrieval matches the task against the description, so it must say precisely what the skill is for.

quiz.question: A successful run that added a UPI payment method took 14 steps, including a 5-step dead end. What should the saved skill contain?
options: All 14 steps, exactly as they happened
The cleaned-up 9 steps that mattered, plus a check
Only the dead end, as a warning
Nothing; one run is not enough to save
quiz.explanation: Distil the working path without detours and end with a check. The dead end can be a one-line warning.

quiz.question: Which metrics show whether a skill library is actually helping? Select all that apply.
options: Average steps per task
Token cost per task
Task success rate
Number of skills stored
quiz.explanation: Outcomes and costs matter. The number of stored skills is a vanity metric.
